title: Social Media and Financial News Manipulation (March 2022 version; a previous version of this paper was titled "Fake News in Financial Markets" / "Fake News: Evidence from Financial Markets")
screen_reason: Finance event study of an SEC investigation into paid-for fraudulent articles on Seeking Alpha. The main analyses (trading-volume and volatility effects) are not prevalence. However, Internet Appendix IA applies a calibrated LIWC-authenticity classifier to the whole downloaded corpus of crowd-sourced financial articles and reports, in Table IA1 Panel A, how many of those articles are classified Fake (5,301), Non Fake (195,232) and Other (150,928) against a stated corpus of 203,545 Seeking Alpha + 147,916 Motley Fool articles. That yields one CONTENT share. The 171 SEC/Pearson articles themselves are an all-false corpus with no denominator and give no row.

estimates.country: United States (U.S.-listed firms; U.S. crowd-sourced financial news platforms)
estimates.platform: Seeking Alpha and Motley Fool (crowd-sourced financial news platforms)
estimates.date: Seeking Alpha articles 2005-2015; Motley Fool articles 2009-2014
estimates.measure_type: % of crowd-sourced financial news articles classified as fake by the authors' calibrated LIWC-authenticity probability model (P(fake) > 20%)
estimates.value_raw: 5,301 Fake / 195,232 Non Fake / 150,928 Other social-media articles (Table IA1 Panel A) out of the downloaded corpus of 203,545 Seeking Alpha + 147,916 Motley Fool articles = 5,301/351,461
estimates.denominator: all articles the authors downloaded from the two platforms: 203,545 Seeking Alpha articles (2005-2015) plus 147,916 Motley Fool articles (2009-2014)
estimates.definition: article whose modelled probability of being fake, from the LIWC authenticity score mapped through Bayes rule onto the SEC/Pearson validation sample, exceeds 20%; articles with P(fake) < 1% are 'Non Fake' and the remainder are left unclassified as 'Other'
estimates.misinfo_def: "Our sample of fraudulent articles is about intent to deceive, where the articles contain information that the authors knew at the time to be false" - paid-for promotional articles written to manipulate a stock price
estimates.page_loc: Internet Appendix, Table IA1 Panel A (LIWC variables), 'Social Media Articles' columns
estimates.ground_truth_detail: LIWC 'authenticity' score converted to P(fake) by Bayes rule, calibrated on a validation sample of 171 SEC/Rick-Pearson 'for-sure fake' articles and 334 non-fake articles by the same authors; classification thresholds P(fake)>0.20 (fake) and <0.01 (non-fake). The algorithm is deliberately conservative: on the validation sample it flagged 18 articles as fake of which 17 were truly fake, but left 137 of the 171 known fake articles unclassified, and 64% of that validation sample fell in the ambiguous band. No human coding of the broader corpus.

estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL for an adjudicator, on two counts. (1) R8: the paper never prints this percentage. The numerator (5,301) and both platform corpus counts are verbatim, and 5,301+195,232+150,928 = 203,545+147,916 = 351,461 exactly, so the whole is fully determined - but obtaining it needs a sum across the three classification bins, which a strict reading of R8 ('never keep a cross-category sum') would forbid. Drop the row if the strict reading is preferred. (2) The estimate is a classifier lower bound, not a measured prevalence: the threshold was chosen to minimise type II errors and left 43% of the corpus ('Other') unclassified, and on the validation sample it caught only 34 of 171 known-fake articles. year=2010 is the midpoint of the 2005-2015 Seeking Alpha span (Motley Fool 2009-2014); no single collection date exists. denom_scope=topical because the corpus is the entire output of two finance-only platforms; sampling_frame=full_census because all articles were downloaded rather than sampled.

missed_or_uncertain: Deliberately not extracted: (a) the 171 fraudulent articles by 20 authors about 47 firms - an all-false corpus supplied by a whistle-blower and the SEC with no denominator, explicitly excluded by the instructions; likewise the 111/147 component counts. (b) The validation-sample composition (171 fake vs 334 non-fake by the same authors, i.e. 33.9%) - a matched case-control design, not a prevalence sample. (c) 'we classify 18,361 of Mr. Jayson's articles as reliably (99% probable) non-fake and only 2 of his articles (0.006%) as probabilistically fake' - a verbatim share, but it is a purposively chosen negative-control author (a full-time Motley Fool journalist selected because he is unlikely to have written fake articles), his exact article total is given only as 'over 31,000', and 38.8% of his articles are unclassified; pooling it would be misleading, so no row was made. An adjudicator wanting maximum recall could add it as a single_source row. (d) All market-effect estimates (4.1% and 23.5% declines in retail trading volume, 1.3% volatility drop, 55% volume increase, 13% price rise reversing to -5%, average P(fake) of 44.51% for flagged articles) - effect sizes and mean probabilities, not shares of misinformation. (e) The 64%/36% ambiguous-vs-classified split refers to the 505-article validation sample. NOTE ON IDENTITY: the manifest title is 'Fake News: Evidence from Financial Markets'; the text is the March 2022 version of the same study by Kogan, Moskowitz & Niessner, retitled 'Social Media and Financial News Manipulation', which states 'A previous version of this paper was titled, "Fake News in Financial Markets."' Same authors, same 171-article SEC sample, same platforms - treated as the same paper, not a wrong text.

rob.design: Event study around the March 2014 SEC investigation, using a full download of two crowd-sourced financial platforms (203,545 Seeking Alpha articles 2005-2015; 147,916 Motley Fool articles 2009-2014, covering 7,700 firms) merged with CRSP/TAQ market data; no sampling and no response rate. The 'for-sure fake' case definition is external and legally grounded (articles supplied by whistle-blower Rick Pearson and subpoenaed by the SEC: 171 articles, 20 authors, 47 firms), but it is a convenience set of detected fraud, not a random sample of fake content. Corpus-wide classification is fully automated (LIWC authenticity -> Bayes-calibrated P(fake)) with no human coding and no inter-coder reliability; classification error is reported only on the 505-article validation sample (17 of 18 flagged articles truly fake; 137 of 171 fake articles missed). Placebo tests (institutional trading, WSJ/NYT articles, filings and press releases) support the event-study design but do not bear on prevalence.
